1.goal: To open on the task, not on the grammar. The grammar is what the task will need.
1.interaction: T–S, one line read out loud. No discussion here.
run: Read the subtitle out loud with her and go straight to the next screen.
Do not name a tense.
1.expected: Nothing to produce yet. She should arrive at the next screen expecting to tell something, not to study something.
1.support: If she asks what the lesson is about, answer with the task: telling a colleague what happened in a class.
1.challenge: Ask which class she is going to tell you about, so she arrives at the next screen already choosing.
1.monitoring: Whether she reaches for grammar on her own. If she does, note it — it is the habit this lesson works against.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The measurement starts on the next screen.

2.goal: To see how she reports a classroom moment before anything is taught. DO NOT CORRECT on this screen.
2.interaction: S talks; you listen and take notes. No correction, no reformulation.
run: She tells you ONE moment from a class she has observed — real or invented.
Let it run.
Take notes on the verb forms, and on where description turns into judgment.
2.expected: Alternative forms are valid. What you are recording is not right or wrong: it is what is AVAILABLE to her without support.
2.support: If she asks “is that right?”, say you will come back to it — and come back to it in stage 4, with her own sentence.
2.challenge: Ask for a second moment from the same class, to see whether the forms hold twice.
2.monitoring: This is the first half of that observation. Where the scene stops and the event starts, and whether a verdict arrives inside the description.
2.evidence: Her sentence, VERBATIM. You need it in stage 4 and again at the end — the lesson becomes visible in the difference.
2.transition: Move on when one moment has been told, whole.

3.goal: To put both forms in front of her in someone else's writing, before any analysis.
3.interaction: S reads alone, then T–S on one question.
run: She reads the note once and answers the question on screen.
The question is about the WRITER, not about grammar.
3.expected: Someone who was in the room, taking notes as it happened, and who is careful about what he is claiming.
3.support: Ask which sentence he would have had to be in the room to write.
3.challenge: Ask which line of the note she would have written differently, and what she would have kept.
3.monitoring: Whether she reads for the writer's position or slips into commenting on the class. The position is what carries the forms.
3.evidence: How she describes the writer — it is the same stance her own report has to take in stage 7.
3.transition: Move on when she has said something about the writer's position, not about tenses.

4.goal: For her to sort the sentences by what they DO, and only then to name the pattern.
4.interaction: S classifies on screen, then T–S before the reveal.
run: She classifies the six, then Check.
Only after that, the question and the reveal — and she answers before you open it.
4.support: Ask, for each one: was this already true before the moment you are describing? If yes, it is the scene.
4.challenge: Ask her to rewrite number 3 so that the teacher who taught the class could not disagree with it.
4.monitoring: Number 3 is the one that matters. It looks like a description and it is a judgment — the teacher who taught the class could disagree with it, and could not disagree with the others.
4.evidence: Whether she separates evaluation from description before being told the categories.
4.transition: Move on when she can say WHY 3 is different, in her own words, before you name anything.

5.goal: To systematize only what the task needs: two past forms and one contrast.
5.interaction: T–S over the table, then her own sentence against it.
run: Go through the table with her.
Then take HER sentence from stage 1 — the one you wrote down verbatim — and put it against the table together. That is the moment the lesson turns from a rule into her own language.
Do NOT present the other past forms. This lesson needs two, and the rest is a different lesson.
Pronunciation: the weak “were”. Stressed, it sounds like she is correcting the other person; unstressed, it disappears into the scene, which is where it belongs.
exact: The two CCQs, in this order: “Which of the two was already happening before the other one started?” and “Did it finish?”
5.expected: The contrast is aspect, not time. Both happened; one is being looked at from inside.
5.support: If the contrast will not land, go back to her own sentence and ask which half of it the colleague could picture.
5.challenge: Ask her to say what changes in the meaning if both halves go into the simple past.
5.monitoring: Whether she treats the contrast as a rule about time. If she does, the CCQs are the way back.
5.evidence: How her stage 1 sentence looks against the table — that comparison is the first measure of the lesson.
5.transition: Move on when she can say what each of the two forms is doing in her own sentence.

6.goal: To stabilize the two forms in the same sentence, out loud, before the meaning gets complicated.
6.interaction: S completes on screen, then says each sentence out loud to you.
run: She completes the four, then says each one out loud.
Correct the FORM here — this is the one stage where that is the point.
6.expected: Scene in the continuous, event in the simple. Any verb she chooses is fine.
6.support: If everything comes out continuous, that is over-correction, not progress. Ask which of the two was cut short.
6.challenge: Ask for a fifth sentence of her own, said without writing it first.
6.monitoring: Whether the contrast is audible, and whether the weak “were” survives when she speeds up.
6.evidence: In how many of the four the contrast is audible. It is the number to compare with the production stage.
6.transition: Move on when four sentences have been said, with the contrast audible in at least three.

7.goal: The same two forms, now on her own material, still without evaluation.
7.interaction: S writes alone, in note form. You read over the rows, not over her shoulder.
run: She fills the five lines in note form — scene and event only.
No judgments yet: that is the next stage, and keeping them apart here is what makes the difference visible later.
7.expected: Five moments from a class she has actually observed, or one she invents in detail.
7.support: If a judgment leaks in — the pace was too fast — do not delete it: move it to the last column and ask what she SAW that made her think so.
7.challenge: Ask which of the five she would tell first if she had only two minutes with the colleague.
7.monitoring: Whether scene and event stay in separate columns when she is writing fast.
7.evidence: The five rows. They are the notes the production stage runs on, and where the judgments went.
7.transition: Move on when five rows exist, even in fragments.

8.goal: The production. Five moments told to someone who was not there — now WITH her reading of them, marked as hers.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the colleague who did not see the class.
run: Let her run, with her notes in front of her.
Ask for detail exactly twice, word for word, using the two lines below, in that order.
The first asks for the scene; the second forces her to narrate and evaluate at once.
exact: Sorry — what were the others doing while that happened?
And is that what you saw, or what you concluded?
8.expected: Scene and event separate in at least three of the five, and at least one reading marked as hers.
8.support: Offer the first clause and let her finish it. If both forms collapse, drop to two moments — the criterion is contrastive use, not quantity.
8.challenge: Ask for the last moment again without the notes in front of her.
8.monitoring: THE SECOND QUESTION IS THE MEASUREMENT. The hypothesis is that the continuous goes under load, not for lack of the form — so watch what happens to it right after that question.
8.evidence: What the forms do under load, and whether the reading arrives marked as a reading. Write one sentence down as she said it.
8.transition: Move on when the five moments have been told and both questions have been answered.

9.goal: Two points from what she said, and ONE moment rebuilt.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the four fields together, then a short retask.
run: Fill the board with her.
Put her own sentence in the third field, word for word — and if it is the sentence from stage 1, say so: the lesson is visible in the difference.
Then Retask: the same moment, in three clauses — scene, event, reading.
9.expected: The likely point is the verdict that arrived inside a description.
9.support: If nothing needs rebuilding, use the retask for the moment that was hardest to say, not for a mistake.
9.challenge: Ask for the rebuilt moment at the speed she would use with a colleague in the corridor.
9.monitoring: The board starts empty and stays hers. Do not pre-fill it with an error she did not make.
9.evidence: The two fields you fill here reach her Feedback tab — write them so she can act on them alone.
9.transition: Move on when the rebuilt moment has been said out loud once.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and how she felt doing it.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the closing question.
run: She reads the list and ticks what she recognizes.
Do not correct the scale.
Say the homework out loud and never write it on the screen.
10.expected: Some of the lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence scale.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which line she could use in the next observation she has booked.
10.challenge: Ask when the next lesson she observes is, and which phrase she would take into it.
10.monitoring: A high mark on the first line and a low one on the third is the hypothesis written by her own hand — the form is there, and the load is what takes it.
10.evidence: Her own confidence reading against what you heard under the second question of stage 8. Fill the post-lesson record before you close.
